statement: SMS is built end-to-end in TypeScript: a Node.js sync worker, a Node.js/Express API, and a React web front end, sharing one type-checked codebase.
The monorepo requires Node.js 22 or later and npm 10 or later.
The API is an Express 4 application using the 'mssql' (Tedious) driver to talk to SQL Server, argon2 for password hashing, zod for input validation, and puppeteer-core for PDF rendering.
The web front end is built with React 18 and Vite 5, with no other UI framework dependency.
The sync worker uses the same 'mssql' driver and zod validation library as the API, kept as a separate workspace package that the API also imports.
A command-line tool ('sms' CLI) exists as its own workspace package for sync/verify/summary/rebuild/user-management operations.
Automated tests use the Vitest test runner; a jsdom-based component harness renders React screens under test.
SMS requires a Microsoft SQL Server instance for its own application database (the 'sidecar'); SQL Server Express, already common on a plant PC, is sufficient and free.
source: CLAUDE.md (Tech stack — D1 app/sidecar DB engine)

statement: The application is designed to run on a Windows PC (Windows Services for the two background processes, Windows-native TLS certificate generation documented), consistent with a plant-floor Windows environment.
Exporting reports to PDF requires Microsoft Edge to be installed on the host machine; SMS drives Edge's own print engine via puppeteer-core rather than bundling a browser.

Choosing to drive the locally installed Edge rather than a bundled Chromium download is explicitly because the target plant PC is air-gapped (no internet access) and a package-install-time browser download would fail there.

SMS looks for Edge in the standard Windows install locations (Program Files, Program Files x86, per-user LocalAppData) or a configurable override path, and reports whether Edge was found as a startup/health fact rather than only failing at export time.

The documented production install method for the two background processes (the sync worker and the API) is NSSM (Non-Sucking Service Manager) registering each as a Windows Service, with auto-start, restart-on-crash, dependency on the SQL Server service, and log rotation.
node-windows is mentioned in documentation as an alternative service-install method to NSSM, but the worked example and the one actually documented step by step is NSSM.
In production the API also serves the built React single-page app, so the browser only needs to reach one service/port (same-origin, no separate web server or CORS configuration needed).

SMS reads production data from the plant's existing SQL Server acquisition database (referred to in code as DATA_TP1U2) and its associated product-master database (PDAS_TP1U2) — the same databases the vendor's own weighing and labelling system already writes.

The connection SMS uses to read the plant's acquisition data is configured as read-only by design, on a dedicated login separate from any writer login (IFL_DB_USER=sms_readonly in the environment template).

SMS copies data from the plant's source database into its own local application database ('sidecar') rather than reading the plant database directly from the web app; the API itself holds no connection to the plant's source database except through the one PDAS write path.

The one-way copy step (the 'sync worker') polls the source database on a configurable interval, default 60 seconds, and reads new rows past a saved position ('watermark') per table rather than re-reading the whole table each time.

Each sync pass re-reads a small overlap of already-seen rows (configurable, default 500) behind the saved watermark, as a safety margin against late-arriving or reordered rows, rather than assuming strict insertion order.

Data flows in one direction only for production readings — from the plant's acquisition database into SMS's own database — never the reverse; the only exception, described separately, is the optional PDAS product-master write path.

Moving SMS from a development copy of the data to the live plant server is designed to be a configuration change only — repointing the sync worker's source connection string — with no change to the API or web application.

SMS's own application database is a separate SQL Server database it fully owns, holding canonical production/reject/sack data derived from the source, plus SMS-specific tables (users, sessions, audit log, product limit history, data-quality findings, sync run history).
source: CLAUDE.md (Tech stack D1); sms/db/migrations (file list, see requirements-map for table inventory)

statement: A repository-wide search for PLC/industrial-protocol client libraries (snap7, Modbus, OPC-UA, S7 protocol libraries) in every package.json and every TypeScript source file found zero matches — no such dependency exists anywhere in the codebase.
source: grep across sms/**/package.json and sms/**/*.ts for snap7|modbus|opc-ua|opcua|s7-1500|nodes7 — zero hits, run against this repository

statement: A documented, disabled configuration stub exists for a possible future direct PLC connection (host/rack/slot settings, an enable flag defaulting to false), but no code reads or acts on these settings today — it is a placeholder for a future phase, not working functionality.
Direct PLC/machine connectivity is explicitly out of scope for the current proposal; SMS reads production data from the plant's existing SQL Server database only, never from the PLCs themselves.

SMS can optionally write product-master changes (new products, retiring products, changing weight limits, new blend/count/tube-type reference values, new pallet records) into the plant's product-master database, through the vendor's own stored procedures rather than direct table writes wherever such a procedure exists.
The exact vendor procedures the write path calls are: CreateMaterial, SetMaterialStatusActive, AddBlend, AddCount, AddTubeType, CreatePallet, and SetPalletStatusActive.

For changing an existing product's weight limits, the vendor supplies no stored procedure at all, so SMS performs one parameterised, single-row UPDATE on the product table and writes a matching event-log row in the vendor's own log format, so the change is visible in the vendor's own audit trail too.
This product-master write path uses its own separate database login, distinct from the read-only login used for production data, and is disabled by a configuration flag that defaults to off.

Only signed-in accounts at or above a specific role rank can trigger the product-master write path; the web screen for it explains and disables itself, stating the reason, whenever the flag is off or a role is insufficient.

The product-master write path touches only six specific vendor tables — Materials, Blends, Counts, TubeTypes, Pallets, and the vendor's own event-log table (nhs_events) — and is designed to never issue a DELETE, never touch any other table, and never write to the plant's cone/sack acquisition database or to any PLC.

The vendor's own product-creation procedure refuses to create a duplicate blend/count/tube-type combination even if a prior product with that combination has since been retired — meaning 'retire and re-create with a new setpoint' is not a workable way to change a product's target weight in the vendor's system; SMS's design instead treats a limit change as an edit to the existing product record.
The web application presents seven main navigation sections: Line, Readings, Weight, Rejects, Sacks, Product, and Report.
The Line screen gives the current/latest status of the production line — a live picture of running/stopped state, current shift, and per-machine activity.
source: sms/web/src/screens/Line.tsx (file exists; see CLAUDE.md floor-first rework and redesign sections)

statement: The Readings screen is a register of individual cone-weight readings, filterable and viewable as a detailed list.
The Weight screen shows cone-weight statistics per station/machine — mean, variation, and comparison to target — built as one shared station table used consistently across the app.
The Rejects screen shows rejected-cone history and trend information, split by reject code/reason.
The Sacks screen shows sack-level data (weight, pass/fail, timestamp) and a line-level sack production ledger by shift/day.

The Product screen has four tabs: Running (what product is currently set per machine), Changeover (the guided workflow to create/retire a product or change its limits), Catalogue (the product master list from PDAS), and History (a log of every product change attempted or made).
The Report screen generates the full set of report types (see report-types facts) as on-screen views and as downloadable Excel/PDF/CSV files.

A Health screen (or Health block within Setup) reports the sync process's own health: whether new data is arriving on schedule, any data-quality findings, and system history (past sync runs, past database rebuild events, past manual verification runs).
A Setup screen, restricted to the admin role, lets an administrator configure line/machine names, sources, reject-code meanings, and weight/shift rules.
source: sms/web/src/screens/Setup.tsx; sms/web/src/screens/setup/ (LineBlock.tsx, MachinesBlock.tsx, RejectCodesBlock.tsx, RulesBlock.tsx, SourcesBlock.tsx, StationsBlock.tsx)

statement: A full-screen 'Wall' display mode exists, intended for a shared TV/monitor on the floor, showing large-type live figures with no navigation chrome.
Account and Login screens handle sign-in and self-service session/password management.

SMS's report service defines a fixed list of report types generated from the canonical data, including a daily report, a shift report, a cone-weight report, a reject report, a sack report, a station report, a product report, a machine/product-by-shift report, a summary report, and a calibration report; and, under IFL's own names from its 29 Sep 2026 email, the eight reports Shift-wise CTS Loop Production, List of Rejected Cones Against Weight, Rejected Sack Report - Daily, SPS Production Report - Count-wise Packing at Each SPS, SPS Sack Weight Range Report, Sack Packing Weight Summary, Rejected Cone Hangers Report and Rejected Unknown (Lifter) Report. Eighteen report types in all.
source: sms/api/src/services/reports/common.ts (REPORT_TYPES, REPORT_TITLES); sms/api/src/services/reports/ (daily.ts, shift.ts, coneWeight.ts, reject.ts, sack.ts, station.ts, product.ts, machineProduct.ts, summary.ts, calibration.ts, shiftProduction.ts, rejectedCones.ts and the six IFL-list report files)

statement: IFL confirmed wanting the tenth report type — production by machine and shift — as the concrete answer to what 'sack stock per machine' should mean, given that individual sacks carry no machine identifier in the source data. That report counts cones per machine (it cannot count sacks per machine); see F058.

Reports can be exported as CSV, as a formatted Excel (.xlsx) workbook with charts and data-bar formatting built by a dependency-free in-house writer, and as a PDF rendered by driving a real browser engine (Microsoft Edge) against the same report page a user would see on screen.
The Excel export includes real charts and formatting elements (not just numbers in a grid), built without a third-party Excel library dependency.

The PDF export reuses the same on-screen report layout and print stylesheet rather than maintaining a separate PDF template, so the three output formats (screen, spreadsheet, PDF/print) cannot drift out of sync with each other.

IFL asked for reports in both Excel and PDF, described as needing to be 'beautiful... with graphics' — this requirement is recorded as answered and the corresponding export code exists; whether the actual output meets IFL's aesthetic bar is something only IFL can judge by reviewing it.

SMS applies statistical process control methods to weight readings: control-chart-style analysis, Nelson rules (a named, standard set of control-chart out-of-control pattern tests), per-station drift detection, and a projection of the number of days until a station's drift reaches its action limit at the current trend.

This calibration advisory is implemented as classical statistics (control charts, Nelson rules, linear drift/projection), not as a machine-learning or AI model — IFL's request for 'AI-based' recommendations is met with a statistical method that produces comparable practical advice ('this station is drifting, expect it to reach its action limit in about N days'), and the parties have not yet agreed whether this satisfies the 'AI' wording of the original requirement.
source: CLAUDE.md ('On the AI expectation'); IFL-QUESTIONS-STATUS.md Q46-48 section

statement: IFL confirmed the calibration feature should be a recommendation only, never an automatic adjustment to a machine, and that no automatic-adjustment approval workflow is needed.

The calibration/drift analysis and reject-trend graphs are shown on the Weight and Rejects screens and in the Calibration report; a manual calibration-adjustment log lets an engineer record when and by how much a station was adjusted.

The plant's own sack data contains only a sack number, a weight, a pass/fail flag, and a timestamp — no machine, station, product, lot, or pallet identifier is recorded per sack, in any data sample examined.
Because of this, SMS cannot compute a per-machine sack stock/ledger directly from the plant's source data — this is a limitation of the source data itself, not of SMS's design.

IFL clarified on 15 Sep 2026 that 'sack stock per machine' should instead mean a production report by machine, by shift and by day. SMS implements cone production per machine by shift and day (the 'Product by machine and shift' report) and sack production at line level by shift, day, product and yarn count; the sack scale records no machine, so sack output cannot be attributed to a machine and no per-machine sack figure or warehouse-style receipts/issues ledger is produced.
source: IFL-QUESTIONS-STATUS.md Q28 section; sms/api/src/services/reports/machineProduct.ts:1-25 (cones per machine, 'Sacks carry no machine'); sms/api/src/services/sacks.ts (sacks at line level)

statement: An optional, manually-entered line-level sack stock ledger also exists in the schema and UI as a secondary feature, in case IFL still wants a manual receipts/issues record after seeing the automatic production report.

SMS does not claim to link a specific sack to the specific cones packed into it, because the source data provides no such key; where the two are shown together, the relationship is presented as an approximation with the limitation stated on screen, never as an exact packing list.
source: CLAUDE.md ('The sack ↔ cone link is approximate and says so')

statement: SMS keeps a time-versioned history of each product's weight limits, so any historical reading is judged against the limit that was actually in force at the time that reading was taken, never against today's current limit.
source: sms/db/migrations/027_product_limit_history.sql; CLAUDE.md ('a reading is judged by the limits in force at its own time')

statement: IFL confirmed that product weight limits should be editable within SMS's own settings, rather than fixed or only mirrored from the vendor system; SMS's local-limits feature lets an engineer-rank user append a new limit version without needing the (separately gated) PDAS write path.

Where the source data itself carries a product identifier on a reading (available since the plant's own database update), SMS uses that identifier directly; for older or unidentified readings, SMS falls back to a manually-set 'current product' selector rather than fabricating an identifier.
source: CLAUDE.md ('Product attribution is real'; Q1/Q15 resolutions)

statement: The plant's acquisition database records a reject/inspection-result code for each rejected cone, but supplies no predefined table of what each code means.

IFL confirmed that reject-code meanings are to be entered by IFL into SMS's own settings screen rather than supplied as a fixed list; SMS provides a dedicated screen and API for an engineer-rank user to name each code.
Until IFL enters these meanings, reject codes display as their raw numeric/textual code rather than a description — this is expected and by design, not a defect.
SMS defines four account roles/ranks: rank 1 viewer, rank 2 engineer, rank 3 manager, rank 4 admin.
source: sms/db/migrations/035_roles_and_answers.sql:8-16 (rename); CLAUDE.md ('Roles are 1 viewer · 2 engineer · 3 manager · 4 admin')

statement: Every signed-in account, at any rank, can view every screen and every report — reading data is not restricted by role. Only specific write actions require a minimum rank.
source: CLAUDE.md ('Every screen is open to every signed-in account')

statement: Setting the currently-running product, logging a calibration adjustment, editing local product weight limits, and entering reject-code meanings all require rank 2 (engineer) or above, matching IFL's own answer that the process engineer on the floor owns these actions.
Exporting the full raw data register requires rank 3 (manager) or above.
Administrative configuration (user accounts, line/machine/station setup, source configuration, weight/shift rules, viewing the audit log) requires rank 4 (admin).

IFL confirmed its user base is a single technical group — the GM, managers, and process/quality engineers — not a mix of technical and non-technical audiences, which is why every screen (not just some) is open to every rank.
source: IFL-QUESTIONS-STATUS.md Q38 section; CLAUDE.md ('The user base is ONE audience')

statement: User passwords are stored as argon2 password hashes, never in plain text; SMS never reuses or reads the plant vendor system's own user table.
source: sms/api/src/auth.ts:2-8; CLAUDE.md (Security section, 'Do not reuse DATA_TP1U2.Users')

statement: Sign-in uses server-side sessions identified by a random session id stored in an httpOnly cookie, not a JSON Web Token and not a value that itself encodes any user data.
A minimum password length is configurable (default 10 characters) and enforced consistently across self-service password change, admin reset, and account creation.

A repeated-failed-login lockout mechanism exists and is protected against a known bypass technique (trusting a spoofable client-supplied IP header) unless the deployment explicitly sits behind a trusted reverse proxy.

Session cookies are marked Secure by default (requiring HTTPS); a documented configuration switch exists for a plain-HTTP plant-intranet deployment, with an explicit warning about the browser behaviour difference between localhost and a LAN IP address.
SMS keeps an append-only audit log table, and a database trigger enforces that it cannot be updated or deleted, not just that the application chooses not to.
source: sms/db/migrations/014_audit_log.sql; sms/.env.example:19-24 (reference to 'the append-only trigger migration 030 puts on sms.audit_log')

statement: Every product change (create, retire, limit change) attempted through SMS — whether it succeeded, failed, or was blocked because the write path was disabled — is recorded in a product-change history table and shown on the Product › History screen.

Because the vendor's own product-master database keeps no record that a limit was ever edited, SMS's own product-change and product-limit-version tables are the only audit trail that will exist for that kind of change.

SMS raises structured data-quality findings, each with a severity level, when it detects a problem such as a stalled sync, an unrecognised source-table generation, or a suspicious/implausible reading — shown on the Health/Operations screen rather than only in a log file.

A command-line 'verify' tool reconciles SMS's own copy of the data against a checksum computed per data generation, and records each run (pass/fail, when it ran) rather than being a one-off manual check with no history.
source: CLAUDE.md ('sms verify reconciles per generation to the checksum'); sms/db/migrations/039_dq_destination_and_verify_run.sql

statement: A reconciliation view compares SMS's own recorded totals against itself as a sanity check; a data-quality finding can be traced back ('destination') to the specific canonical row it concerns, so an operator can jump from a warning to the actual record.
A documented backup script exists for the application database, writing .bak files to a configurable directory; the Health screen reports the age of the newest backup file found there.

A retention policy is configurable and implemented for two specific table categories — old sync-run history rows (default 90 days) and non-critical data-quality finding rows (default 365 days) — always keeping at least the newest row per table.
Raw and canonical production readings, the audit log, and the product-change history are explicitly never pruned by the retention job — they are kept indefinitely.

A comprehensive, IFL-specific backup schedule, off-site/off-machine copy policy, and formal retention SLA are not fully documented as a finished operational policy at this stage — the mechanism exists (backup script, retention job) but the operating policy around it (frequency, off-site copy, responsibility) is a deployment-planning item to finalise with IFL.
source: sms/.env.example:107-116 (mechanism only); no dedicated backup/retention SLA document found in the repository

statement: The API's default listening port is 4000.

The application database and the plant's source database both default to SQL Server's standard TCP port, 1433, in the environment template (adjustable if a site's SQL Server instance uses a non-default port).
An optional direct-TLS configuration is documented (Windows-native PFX certificate or a PEM cert/key pair) for serving the application over HTTPS without a separate reverse proxy.

SMS is accessed through a standard web browser — there is no separate desktop client to install on user workstations; only the server-side PDF export step requires Microsoft Edge to be present on the server host.
IFL confirmed the owner (not IFL) supplies the PC that SMS runs on, with the software already installed, closing the procurement question for the hosting hardware.

IFL confirmed the intended users are the GM, managers, and process/quality engineers, and that the process engineer specifically is the role authorised to change products, weight limits, and sack-related adjustments.
IFL confirmed wanting reports in both Excel and PDF format, described as needing graphics and a polished appearance, generated on both a daily and a per-shift basis for every report type.
IFL confirmed direct PLC communication is out of scope entirely — SMS should read from the existing SQL Server databases only, with no automation or direct machine connection.
IFL confirmed that automatic emailing of reports is not wanted.

IFL confirmed each of the plant's winding machines is itself the same thing as a 'station' (one concept, numbered 1 through 14 on this line) — there is no separate finer-grained spindle/head identification to model.
IFL confirmed weight limits and reject-code meanings are not fixed values to be supplied once, but are to be entered and kept editable by IFL within SMS's own settings screens.
IFL confirmed sack weight is recorded and should be treated as the total (gross) weight of the sack, not a net weight after subtracting tare.

IFL confirmed wanting SMS to be able to add, retire, and edit products in the plant's product-master system on their behalf, replacing today's manual process of writing SQL directly against the vendor database — this is the basis for the PDAS write-path feature.
Formal, written approval of the specific KPI definitions and calculation methods shown on reports is still pending IFL sign-off.
The meaning of each reject/inspection code is still pending IFL data entry into SMS's own settings screen — the feature to enter it exists, but the meanings themselves have not yet been supplied.
The precise weight basis for cone weight (as-recorded vs. gross vs. net) remains an open confirmation with IFL, distinct from the sack weight basis question, which IFL has already answered.
source: IFL-QUESTIONS-STATUS.md Q24 section (sack weight resolved) vs. cone weight basis unconfirmed note in same section

statement: A dedicated read-only database login and connection details for the live plant server have not yet been provided and are required before installation can proceed.
Complete, continuous historical production data covering the full period IFL wishes to report on has not yet been confirmed as available, and is to be requested from and supplied by IFL.
source: IFL-QUESTIONS-STATUS.md Q56 section (generic statement; no dates or figures reproduced here)

statement: Whether the statistical calibration-advisory feature satisfies the original requirement's wording of 'AI-based' analytics has not yet been explicitly agreed with IFL, even though the underlying feature and its scope (recommendation-only) have been agreed.

Formal, written confirmation from IFL authorising the optional product-master write path, covering each of the specific write operations, is required before that path is enabled against the live database; this confirmation is still being finalised as a project/process matter, separate from the technical readiness gate applied before the feature is switched on.
source: CLAUDE.md ('Current phase' section, PDAS write authority); CLAUDE.md hard constraint 3

statement: SMS records a full timeline of which product was running on which machine over time (an append-only history), not just the currently active product, supporting historical/product-wise reporting from the point the source data began carrying a product identifier.

SMS reports the health of its own data pipeline using the age of the OLDEST source table's freshest reading, not just the newest, so a partially-stalled data feed cannot be masked by other tables still updating normally.
source: CLAUDE.md ('live.ts reports ... freshness from the OLDEST source table')

statement: When the sync health check is not able to confirm the line is running normally, screens are designed to avoid asserting a definite running/stopped state rather than guessing.
source: CLAUDE.md (UI redesign rule 4, 'THE HEALTH DECISION IS SERVER-SIDE AND MEASURED')

statement: SMS distinguishes 'the scale's own pass/fail flag on a reading' from 'whether that reading falls within the tolerance of the product that was actually running at that time' as two separate, separately-labelled facts, rather than silently applying today's tolerance to old readings.

SMS treats the plant's own recorded production timestamps and its own internally-generated timestamps as two distinct clocks, converting between them explicitly, because a fixed time-zone-like offset separates the two in the environments observed so far.
source: CLAUDE.md (UI redesign rule 2, 'TWO CLOCKS, NAMED'); sms/.env.example:139-164 (PLANT_UTC_OFFSET_MINUTES)

statement: SMS checks, at startup, whether the deployment host's own operating-system time zone matches the configured plant time-zone offset, and raises a warning (visible on the Operations screen) if they disagree, rather than assuming the host was configured correctly.

Every screen anchors its notion of 'now' and its time-period selector on the plant's own clock as reported by the API, not the viewing browser's local clock, so a device with an incorrect clock cannot mis-state what period is being viewed.

Every canonical record carries a line identifier (line_id) throughout the schema, which is the mechanism intended to let SMS extend to additional production lines/machines in future, though only a single line's configuration has been built and exercised so far.
source: CLAUDE.md (requirement mapping table, 'Scalable to more machines and data points')

statement: Dispatch tracking is not part of the current proposal; IFL confirmed no dispatch data exists in the source systems and dispatch was explicitly confirmed out of scope.
SMS is designed to run entirely on the plant's local intranet with no cloud dependency, consistent with an air-gapped plant PC.
source: CLAUDE.md (Security section, 'Deployment target is the plant intranet, no cloud dependency')

topic: Data model — no schema changes to source
statement: SMS's design commits to making zero schema, index, table, procedure, or data modifications to the plant's own cone/sack acquisition database; all optimisation and additional structure lives in SMS's own database.
All database queries in the codebase are written as parameterised queries rather than string-concatenated SQL, as a working rule applied throughout.
source: CLAUDE.md (Working rule 3) — stated as a standing project rule; not independently re-verified line-by-line across every query in this pass

statement: Database and other credentials are supplied only via environment variables/configuration files that are excluded from version control, never hardcoded in source.
source: sms/.env.example (template only, real .env excluded); CLAUDE.md (Working rule 1)
